newsitem.title: INDIA: Meeting will tout Asian infrastructure investment.
newsitem.headline: Meeting will tout Asian infrastructure investment.

text.p: Government ministers from 30 Asian nations will meet with private firms and seek investment commitments in regional infrastructure during a rare dialogue in New Delhi this week, United Nations officials said on Sunday.

"The ministers will be questioned by the private sector. It will be like a dialogue. It is the first of its kind," a spokesman for the U.N. Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (ESCAP), told Reuters.
Four days of meetings kick off on Monday with a two-day conference of ministers from 51 ESCAP nations to be inaugurated by Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda.
ESCAP has estimated that developing countries in the Asia-Pacific region needed $1.5 trillion in new infrastructure development between 1993 and 2000, of which $500 billion has been committed.
That leaves $1 trillion in additional projects, many of which will be dependent on private investors, ESCAP says.

Private-sector infrastructure experts say governments must share risks, frame suitable laws, and develop financial arrangements to help the private sector in a field where investments are high but returns take years to materialise.
They say pricing of infrastructure services is another crucial issue that needs to be considered by policy-makers.

"There are today no legal and financial engineering skills in the government," said K. Ramchand, a senior official of India's Infrastructure Leasing and Financial Services Ltd (IL&FS), an infrastructure management company.
"I think we are going to get a whole lot of examples from other areas, and a sharing of experiences (at the meetings)."
ESCAP officials say they expect Malaysia, which has successfully used the build-operate-transfer (BOT) method of getting projects built, to serve as an example to others.
Experts say countries like India need billions of dollars to build roads, ports, bridges and power plants, without which their ambitions of high economic growth may be hindered.
"Unless something is done, one day things could come to a standstill," said Ritu Gupte, strategist at investment bank Jardine Fleming.

During the conference, the ESCAP ministers will join with private-sector participants in launching the Alliance for Infrastructure Development in Asia (AIDA), a forum involving private firms and government agencies.
AIDA's launch will coincide with the unveiling of a list of Asian-Pacific infrastructure projects open to private investors that was formulated last week by officials from ESCAP countries.

AIDA member nations also will issue a joint declaration on perceived challenges to infrastructure development. ESCAP officials last week called for transparency in government procedures for bidding out infrastructure projects. The issue is expected to figure in the ministerial discussions

Following the ministerial conference, private-sector participants will hold a separate meeting on Wednesday and Thursday called the World Infrastructure Forum, which will address ways of promoting infrastructure investment worldwide.
The Singapore-based AIDA will bring together multilateral agencies like the Asian Development Bank and the World Bank with governments and private firms, an ESCAP official said.
